items.title: 1.10 Variation in oxidation number in oxides and chlorides

source_refs.note: Topic 1.10, printed page 18, as printed: oxidation numbers in period 3 oxides and chlorides, Table 1.2 and Quick Check 1.9.

blocks.text: The oxidation number of an atom is the formal charge on that atom in a molecule or ion. The oxidation number is also referred to as the oxidation state. In ionic compounds the oxidation number of an atom is defined as the charge which appears on the ions.
Let’s examine the oxidation numbers in oxides and chlorides of the third period.

The oxidation number of an element of 3rd Period in its oxide or chloride corresponds to the number of electrons used for bonding and is always positive because oxygen and chlorine are more electronegative than any of these elements. The oxidation number matches the group number, reflecting the total number of valence electrons. Consider the following table (Table 1.2) for oxidation states of various elements of the periodic table. In the oxides, the oxidation number increases from +1 in Na to +6 in S. In chlorides, the oxidation number increases from +1 in Na to +5 in P. Phosphorus and sulfur exhibit several oxidation numbers because they can expand their octet by exciting electrons into empty 3d orbitals.
book_errors: The oxidation number matches the group number, reflecting the total number of valence electrons.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: This holds only with the old group numbering (groups 1–7). With the 1–18 numbering used in this chapter, the highest oxidation number of a period 3 element equals its number of valence electrons: the group number for groups 1 and 2, and the group number minus 10 for groups 13–17 (e.g. Al +3 in group 13, S +6 in group 16).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the oxidation number of S in SCl₂ as -2. It is +2: each Cl is -1 and the molecule is neutral, and period 3 elements always have positive oxidation numbers in their chlorides.

For instance, in SO₂, sulfur has an oxidation number of +4 because only four electrons are used for bonding, while in SO₃, sulfur has an oxidation number of +6 because all six electrons are used for bonding.

blocks.prompt: a) Calculate the oxidation number of sulphur in SO₂ and SO₃.
blocks.explanation: Each oxygen is −2 and the molecule is neutral. SO₂: x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4. SO₃: x + 3(−2) = 0, so x = +6.

blocks.prompt: b) Why some p block elements show variable oxidation state.
blocks.explanation: Period 3 elements such as phosphorus and sulphur have empty 3d orbitals. By exciting electrons into these 3d orbitals they can use more or fewer valence electrons for bonding, so phosphorus shows +3 or +5 and sulphur +4 or +6.
